1fctfHw2eyI.transcript: In 1869, two men digging a well in New York hit something hard, about 3 feet down. It was a giant, a 10-foot-tall stone man lying in the dirt. Within days, crowds were lining up to see it. There was just one problem. It was fake, and the man who made it was laughing all the way to the bank. His name was George Hull, and he sold tobacco for a living. He was also an atheist, which made him the odd man out in his town. One day, he got into a big argument with a Methodist preacher. The preacher said that every word in the Bible was literally true, including the line about giants walking the earth. George thought that was ridiculous, and then he thought of a way to prove his point and maybe make some money while he was at it. His plan, if people were going to believe in giants, he would give them a giant. So he had a huge block of stone carved into a man about 10 feet tall and weighing around 3,000 pounds. Then he made it look old. He scratched and scuffed it until it looked like it had been underground for ages. Next, he needed somewhere to hide it. He asked his cousin, a farmer named William Newell, who agreed to bury it on his farm in Cardiff, New York. And there it sat underground for a whole year. George spent over $2,600 on all of this, which was a lot of money back then. Then one day, Newell told some workers to dig a well in exactly the spot where the giant was waiting. They dug down and their shovels hit stone. They brushed off the dirt and saw a huge stone man staring back at them. The workers ran for help, and the word spread fast. Newell put up a tent over the giant and charged people to come and look up to 50 cents ahead. People came from all over, in wagons and on foot, and everyone had a theory. Some said it was an ancient man who had turned to stone. Others said it was a statue made long ago by missionaries. A professor from Yale took a close look, saw chisel marks, and said a fake, but nobody wanted to hear that because the line for the tent kept getting longer. Meanwhile, George just watched with a very big smile. Soon, a group of businessmen bought the giant, paying much more than it had cost to make and moved it to the city of Syracuse, where even more people lined up. Then a very famous showman heard about it. P.T. Barnum, the king of circus tricks, offered $60,000 to borrow the giant for 3 months. The owner said no. Well, Barnum did not like being told no, so he did what any good showman would do. He built his own giant, a copy made of plaster, which he put on display in New York City and told everyone that his was the real one. Now the owners of the first giant were furious. Imagine that, a fake giant copied by another fake giant. So they took Barnum to court, but the judge had a problem with that. He said the owners would first have to prove their giant was real or, as he put it, the giant would have to swear to its own genuineness, which of course a stone man cannot do. TDcdC21gvWc.transcript: The year is 1896. Sultan Hamad, King of Zanzibar and puppet of the British Empire, has just been assassinated, poisoned by his usurper cousin who then declared himself Sultan. The British were determined to not let this stand, and the shortest, yet surprisingly bloody war, the 40-minute long Anglo-Zanzibar War, was about to begin. Sultan Hamad had ruled peacefully for 3 years. Zanzibar was a productive British protectorate under the rule of Hamad bin Thuwaini, a British-backed Sultan. British rule of Zanzibar began in 1890 with the signing of the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty between the United Kingdom and German Empire. This treaty traded control of a few key lands between the two powers. While no one really knows how Thuwaini died, he suddenly took ill with a mysterious illness and was dead within hours. 2 hours after his death, his cousin Khalid bin Bargash seized the palace by force and soon had an army of almost 2,500 armed men, including machine guns, cannons, and an armed sloop surrounding the palace. The British were not happy with this, to say the least. While they could overlook the overthrow of a Sultan, they rightfully guessed that Khalid was unlikely to play ball with the British and that he would be a difficult ruler to control. Hence, they wanted succession to go to Hamoud bin Muhammad, a more pliable leader. At the time of the overthrow, there were two British men-of-war in the harbor of Zanzibar Town under the command of Chief Diplomat Basil Cave. Their marine complements went ashore and began fortifying the consulate. The British first sent for reinforcements, and soon HMS Racoon, St. George, and Sparrow arrived. They also sent a telegraph asking to use force should negotiations fail. The British command's response was simple: "You are authorized to adopt whatever measures you may consider necessary and will be supported in your action by Her Majesty's Government. Do not, however, attempt to take any action which you are not certain of being able to accomplish successfully. In other words, yes, but only if you know you won't fail. Following failed negotiations, an ultimatum was sent to Khalid. Leave the palace by 9:00 a.m. the following day or you will be forced out. He responded with, "We have no intention of hauling down our flag and we do not believe you would open fire on us." Cave sent back, "But unless you do as you are told, we shall certainly do so." Within an hour, the ultimatum had lapsed and the British admiral called his men to general quarters before hoisting their action flag. The Anglo-Zanzibar War had begun. A naval battle began immediately as the men-of-war fired on the Zanzibari sloop, which was quickly overpowered. The men-of-war then turned their guns on the palace and over the next 30 minutes pounded the palace complex into dust, killing 500 of the Zanzibari defenders and sending Khalid fleeing. Just like that, the Anglo-Zanzibar War was over. The shortest war in history lasted just roughly 40 minutes. Khalid was later smuggled out of the country by German friends. However, Hamoud bin Muhammad was installed upon the throne as Sultan of Zanzibar, where he ruled until his death six years later.
